newsitem.title: UK: Mitchell plays down talk of Clinton job offer.
newsitem.headline: Mitchell plays down talk of Clinton job offer.

text.p: Former U.S. senator George Mitchell on Wednesday played down reports that newly re-elected President Bill Clinton might appoint him Secretary of State and said he remained committed to his job at the helm of Northern Ireland peace talks. "If I am offered that or anything else I will consider it at the time but I really don't waste any time or lose any sleep speculating or worrying about it," he told reporters before starting another round of the troubled talks in Belfast.

"I have had no discussions about it with the President...My commitment is here, to do the best I can to contribute in whatever way I can...to the process that is under way in Northern Ireland. I am going to keep at it."

Political sources on both sides of the Irish border added to media speculation that Clinton might bring the experienced Mitchell into his administration in a powerful role following his handling of multi-party talks which has won praise from some of his pro-British critics.
"There has to be a question mark over Mitchell," an Irish diplomat said.

Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the hardline Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) told Reuters: "He may be required to go back to the U.S. to perform some other duty rather than to be Clinton's emissary here."
Britain and Ireland invited Mitchell to chair the talks in June in an effort to establish peace after years of war by rival guerrillas about the future of British rule.
Both governments say that Sinn Fein, the political wing of the resurgent Irish Republican Army, will be given a seat in talks only if the IRA calls a genuine ceasefire.

The IRA went back to war in February after a 17 month truce. Britain and its Protestant supporters in Northern Ireland said it was only a tactical ceasefire. They say republicans must prove they are dedicated to democratic methods.
The uncertainty about Mitchell came as Catholic nationalist parties in both Irelands applauded Clinton's re-election.

Prime Minister John Bruton told the Dublin parliament that Clinton had been a "great, good and consistent friend to Ireland. "We as a country have much to be grateful for in respect of President Clinton's first term," Bruton said.

The Social Democratic and Labour Party, whose leader John Hume is trying to bridge a gap between Britain and Irish republicans and achieve an IRA guerrilla ceasefire, praised Clinton's energy in helping to ease the region's problems.
"The SDLP is delighted at his re-election which is a great boost to the peace process," chairman Jonathan Stephenson said in a statement.
But the DUP said it feared "more interference" by Clinton in the affairs of the province on behalf of Irish nationalists.

Robinson, a staunch critic of what he sees as U.S. meddling in the Northern Irish peace process, said Clinton might step up involvement if the British Labour Party ousts the ruling Conservatives in a general election due next Spring.
"Labour has always welcomed American involvement. The Conservatives haven't, there has always been very considerable resistance on the (Conservative parliamentary) back-benches."
The powerful Protestant Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), which is backed by most of the province's majority Protestants, said its leaders hope to meet Clinton in Washington early next month.

"The people of America have made their choice and chosen to re-elect President Clinton. In fairness to the President, he has taken a greater interest in the Northern Ireland situation than any of his predecessors," UUP spokesman Jeffrey Donaldson said.
"So, in so far as that will continue, we hope that his Administration will continue to be even-handed and balanced in their approach," Donaldson told Reuters.
